# The domino problem is undecidable on the long range graph and the Barbieri–Sablik H-graph

On two Schreier graphs of self-similar groups, the long range graph on the integers and a subgraph of the half-plane, no algorithm decides
whether a finite set of forbidden colored patterns admits a coloring; on post-critically finite self-similar graphs the problem is decidable.

**The domino problem on Schreier graphs.** Let a group $G = \langle A \rangle$ generated by a finite set $A$ act on a set $X$. Its *Schreier graph* has vertex set $X$ and an edge labeled $a$ from $x$ to $a \cdot x$ for each $a \in A$ and $x \in X$. For a finite set $B$ of colors, a
*pattern* is a map $F \to B$ on a finite set $F$ of words over $A^{\pm 1}$. The *domino problem* on a fixed graph asks, given a finite set $B$ of colors and a finite set $\mathscr{F}$ of forbidden patterns over $B$, whether some coloring $\tau : X \to B$ avoids them, that is, for every $x \in X$ and every pattern $\pi : F \to B$ in $\mathscr{F}$,
the map $f \mapsto \tau(f \cdot x)$ differs from $\pi$; for Cayley graphs this is the domino problem of [finitely generated groups](wang-tilings-of-finitely-generated-groups-and-th.md).

**Theorem (Bartholdi).**

1. The domino problem is undecidable on the *long range graph*: the Schreier graph of $A = \{t, u\}$ acting on $\mathbb{Z}$, where $t$ connects $n$ to $n + 1$ for all $n$, and $u$ connects $2^s(2m - 1)$ to $2^s(2m + 1)$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and fixes $0$, giving a loop at $0$ (§5.1 and Theorem B of the source). It is the Schreier graph of a self-similar group of linear activity growth: in the transducer generating that group, the number of paths of length $n$ ending at a non-trivial state grows linearly in $n$ (§1.2 of the source).
2. The domino problem is undecidable on the *Barbieri–Sablik $H$-graph*, a subgraph of the half-plane in which some edges are replaced by loops (Theorem C).
3. For a substitution $s$ on the square grid, the domino problem on the self-similar structure of $s$ (tilings of the grid in which adjacency is enforced only between black squares of the colorings defined by iterating $s$) is undecidable when $s$ contains an *isthmus*,
   a configuration of blocks forming at least two strips in one direction and one in another; this answers a question of Barbieri and Sablik (Theorem 1.1).

Both graphs of items 1 and 2 are Schreier graphs of self-similar groups produced by small transducers. In contrast, the domino problem is decidable on post-critically finite self-similar graphs, Schreier graphs of bounded self-similar groups such as the Sierpiński gasket graphs and those of the Basilica group (Theorem A, = Proposition 4.1), and on such a graph built from an eventually periodic ray the whole monadic second-order theory is decidable (Theorem D, = Theorem 4.2).

## Expansion

The proofs are uniform: a set of forbidden patterns on the graph *simulates a grid*, marking some vertices as vertices of a grid $\Delta$ and some paths of edges as its edges, with signals carried along the edges. Any domino instance on $\Delta$ combined with this simulation
gives a domino instance on the graph, so undecidability transfers from $\Delta$. On the long range graph a seeded coloring simulates an octant of the plane, and the tiling problem on the octant reduces to the seeded tiling problem, which in turn is eliminated; on the
$H$-graph the simulated grid comes from its self-similar structure. For substitutions with an isthmus, the right half of the associated graph is essentially the $H$-graph. A complete expansion links the reduction from the seeded to the unseeded problem and the grid
simulation of Bartholdi and Salo.

Items 2 and 3 name the $H$-graph and the isthmus condition only informally; a complete expansion defines the $H$-graph by its generating transducer (§5.2 of the source) and the isthmus as in Theorem C and Theorem 1.1 before stating them.
